passage:
I'm Meera, the junior analyst, and I saw the pricing fight from my desk. Francis arrived Monday with screenshots of three competitors' price pages. Deepak came Tuesday with a survey sheet and a folder of quotes. By Thursday they were quoting each other's old mistakes, and the price hardly came up.
On Friday Deepak said, "Fine, your number," and shut the laptop. Francis told me afterwards it was good to have it settled.
Since then, in the stand-ups, Deepak just says "nothing from me". I can't tell if that's hurt or just tiredness. Last week I found a half-written plan for a simpler free trial in a shared folder, dated before the pricing fight. Nobody had seen it.
— Meera

qa.q: What did Deepak bring to the discussion on Tuesday?
qa.a: Deepak brought a survey sheet and a folder of quotes.

qa.q: What might Deepak be feeling since giving in on the price?
qa.a: Deepak may be hurt, shown by the flat "nothing from me" in stand-ups, though Meera admits it could be tiredness.

qa.q: What could the founders try next time they disagree about a price?
qa.a: They could agree on what evidence would settle it and run a small test of both prices, so the question is about the customers rather than who is right.

qa.q: Why might Francis feel the debate went well?
qa.a: Francis got a decision and a settled question, and told Meera that was good, without seeing what it cost in Deepak's ideas.

grounding: The account shows two founders gathering proof to win a pricing argument, after which the one who lost stops sharing ideas.

passage:
Monday, 3 March. Vandana and Santosh disagree about pricing their billing software: she wants ₹499 a month, he wants ₹999. By evening each has a folder called "proof". Hers has cheaper competitors. His has three customers who said they'd pay more.
Thursday, 13 March. The pricing meeting lasts two hours. Nobody asks what the other has learned. Vandana wins because their advisor sides with her. "Told you," she says, closing her laptop. Santosh says nothing.
Monday, 21 April. Santosh hasn't suggested a single idea in six weeks. In product meetings he just nods. A customer tells Vandana they would happily pay more for proper reports; Santosh had mentioned that exact feature in February and has not raised it since. Vandana realises she won the argument and lost her co-founder's voice.

qa.q: What did Vandana say after winning?
How did Santosh feel after losing?
qa.a: Santosh likely felt humiliated and shut out, which is why he stopped sharing ideas.

qa.q: What could they have done instead of collecting proof to win?
qa.a: Shared what each had learned, perhaps tested both prices with a few customers, and decided together.

qa.q: How does Vandana see things by April?
qa.a: Vandana realises she won the argument but lost Santosh's ideas, which hurts the company more.

grounding: It shows co-founders gathering proof to win a pricing debate, after which the loser stops sharing ideas, hurting the company more than a wrong price would.

passage:
Joseph sir leaned back when Dilnaz said she had crushed her co-founder in a pricing debate. "Crushed, is it? Sit. When I was twenty-five, my partner Ravi and I ran a tour company in Munnar. We fought about pricing: he wanted cheap packages, I wanted premium. I spent a week collecting every number that proved him wrong. At the meeting I laid them out like a lawyer. I won.
And Ravi went quiet. Not angry, just quiet. For a whole season he didn't suggest a single new route or idea, and Ravi was the one with the ideas. We lost two big school groups that year because nobody thought of a student package. Ravi had mentioned it months before, and I had waved it away in that same meeting.
The price I chose was fine. What I lost was worth far more."

qa.q: How did young Joseph feel after winning the meeting, and later?
qa.a: He probably felt triumphant at first, then regretful when Ravi went quiet and the ideas dried up.

qa.q: Which choice in the story went wrong, and what could have fixed it?
qa.a: Arguing like a lawyer to win; listening to Ravi's ideas, like the student package, could have kept both the price and the partnership healthy.

qa.q: How did Ravi experience losing the debate?
qa.a: Ravi felt dismissed and went quiet, suggesting no new routes or ideas for a whole season.

grounding: It shows a young co-founder winning a pricing argument with collected proof, after which his partner stops sharing ideas and the company loses more than a wrong price would cost.
